openingProblem.problem: In March 1991 most Soviet voters who took part in a referendum voted to keep the Union. Nine months later it no longer existed. Who, or what, ended the Soviet Union: the coup plotters, Yeltsin, the republics, or Gorbachev himself?
openingProblem.predictionPrompt: Your prediction in one line: who ended the Soviet Union?
openingProblem.revisitPrompt: Look back at your prediction. Which piece of evidence most changed or confirmed it?

chunks.title: Two Moscows: Yeltsin and the republics, 1990
chunks.body:
In 1990 the decisive struggle in the Soviet Union moved from the party to the republics, and above all to Russia. Boris Yeltsin, sacked as Moscow party chief in 1987, won a seat in the elections to the Russian Supreme Soviet in March 1990, and on 29 May the Russian Congress of People's Deputies elected him its chairman.

Two weeks later, on 12 June 1990, the Russian congress issued a **Declaration of State Sovereignty**, giving Russian authority precedence over Soviet rule on Russian territory. Seventeen Moments describes the result as a "dual power" like that of 1917: Gorbachev at the head of the Soviet Union, Yeltsin at the head of Russia, in the same city. Similar declarations followed from Moldova, Belarus and Ukraine, whose parliament declared sovereignty in July. Then, on 12 July 1990, at the Twenty-Eighth Party Congress, Yeltsin resigned from the Communist Party, calling it a party of "power thirsty bureaucrats".

Why did this matter so much? Russia had been the only republic without its own Communist Party, and its posts had been relatively unimportant. Yeltsin turned the Russian institutions into a rival centre of power. Judt argues that Gorbachev's "major tactical mistake" in domestic affairs had been to create a national legislature with real powers and national visibility. Yeltsin understood faster than Gorbachev that elected bodies would become a forum for every kind of discontent, and he aligned Russia's interests with those of the other republics. Gorbachev, by contrast, found himself aligned "uneasily and unconvincingly" with officials nostalgic for the party monopoly he had broken.

This mattered because the Soviet Union could survive the loss of the Baltic republics, but not the defection of Russia, which meant that once Russia's leaders claimed sovereignty the Union's centre had no secure territory of its own. By the end of 1990, declarations of sovereignty were coming even from regions inside Russia, such as Tatarstan and Chechnya. Gorbachev's answer in the winter of 1990–91 was to rely on the conservatives. In November he took sweeping powers to rule by decree, and in December his Foreign Minister, Eduard Shevardnadze, resigned without warning, telling the Congress that dictatorship was coming. Within a month riot police were attacking strategic points in the Baltic states.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Russian sovereignty, not Baltic nationalism, was the fatal blow to the centre, because Russia was the Union's core.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The Baltic and Georgian movements came first and set the example Russia followed.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Yeltsin's break with the party gave him a popular base Gorbachev lacked.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: In 1990 Yeltsin was elected chairman by deputies, not the people; his popular mandate came only in June 1991.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Gorbachev's turn to the right in winter 1990–91 cost him the reformers without winning the conservatives.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: He abandoned it in April 1991, so it was a phase rather than a final choice.

chunks.title: The last attempt to save the Union, March–August 1991
chunks.body:
Gorbachev's strategy in 1991 was to replace the old Union with a new, looser one by agreement. On 17 March 1991 a referendum asked whether voters wanted to preserve the USSR "as a renewed federation of sovereign republics". An overwhelming majority of those voting said yes. But six republics, the three Baltic states, Armenia, Georgia and Moldavia, refused to take part, and in April Georgia declared independence. Even the yes votes were ambiguous: in Ukraine over 70 per cent supported the revised Union, but nearly 80 per cent also approved Ukraine's own declaration of sovereignty.

April brought crisis. Miners had been on strike since March, demanding Gorbachev's resignation, and Prime Minister Pavlov's price rises of 2 April provoked further strikes. Gorbachev could have used force, as in Vilnius earlier in the year. Instead he abandoned his "turn to the right". Judt notes that in April he reluctantly conceded to the republics the right of secession in a new Union constitution. On 23 April he met the leaders of the nine republics that had taken part in the referendum, including Yeltsin, at Novo-Ogarevo outside Moscow, and they agreed to draft a new treaty: the "nine plus one" agreement.

Meanwhile Yeltsin's position grew stronger. On 12 June 1991 he was elected President of the Russian republic, in Judt's words "the first ever democratically chosen leader of Russia". Gorbachev had been chosen President of the USSR by the Congress, not by the voters, so for the first time the Russian leader had a popular mandate that the Soviet leader could not match.

On 12 July the USSR Supreme Soviet voted for a new, decentralised Union. The treaty, published on 14 August and due to be signed on 20 August, gave the republics ownership of virtually all natural resources on their territory, made republic laws supreme over Union laws, and replaced "Socialist" with "Sovereign" in the country's name. This mattered because the centre was signing away its economic and legal supremacy, which meant that conservatives in the leadership now saw 20 August as the last date on which the old Union could be saved. Judt observes that Gorbachev's concessions convinced his conservative foes that he "would have to be removed if order was to be restored".

argumentsThatWork.claim: Gorbachev tried to save the Union by giving most of its power away: the treaty made the republics supreme.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Without such concessions the nine republics would not have signed at all.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The yes vote was real: an overwhelming majority of participating voters backed a renewed federation.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Yeltsin's popular election in June 1991 shifted legitimacy from the Union to Russia.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Yeltsin still took part in the Novo-Ogarevo process, so he had not yet abandoned a Union.

chunks.title: The August coup: why did it fail?
chunks.body:
The coup was timed to stop the Union Treaty from being signed on 20 August. Its leaders formed an eight-member **State Committee for the State of Emergency**: among them KGB chairman Vladimir Kryuchkov, Defence Minister Dmitrii Yazov, Prime Minister Valentin Pavlov, Interior Minister Boris Pugo and Vice-President Gennadii Yanaev. Several were men Gorbachev had appointed himself and relied on during his turn to the right. When Gorbachev, on holiday in the Crimea, refused to cooperate, the committee announced on 19 August that he could not exercise his authority "for health reasons". Yanaev signed a decree stripping him of power and a six-month state of emergency was declared. Tanks entered Moscow.

The coup collapsed within three days. Its first weakness was its own support. Judt notes that a majority of senior KGB officers refused to back Kryuchkov, and Seventeen Moments records that the soldiers and elite KGB units sent into the streets refused to fire on or disperse the demonstrators. Judt adds that the plotters were clear about what they were against but never able to say what they were for. The very need to declare an emergency merely to replace one Communist leader with another, he argues, showed how far the old structures had unravelled.

The second weakness was Boris Yeltsin. On 19 August he denounced the takeover as an illegal coup and placed himself at the head of the resistance in the Russian Parliament building, the White House, climbing onto a tank before the cameras to rally its defenders. Thousands of Muscovites surrounded the building. Yeltsin telephoned world leaders, who gave him their support and withheld recognition from the plotters. The resistance was not without cost: on the night of 20–21 August three demonstrators died in clashes with the army.

The third weakness was that the republics did not wait. On 20 August Estonia declared independence, and Latvia followed the next day. By 21 August the plotters had given up; Pugo committed suicide and the others were arrested. Gorbachev flew back to Moscow. This mattered because the coup had been defeated not by Gorbachev but by Yeltsin and the crowd, which meant that its failure transferred authority from the Union to Russia. Seventeen Moments compares it to Kornilov's coup of 1917: in both cases the failed attempt benefited not the government but those who could claim credit for stopping it.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The coup failed mainly because the armed forces and the KGB would not use force for it.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Three demonstrators did die, so force was used, though not decisively.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Yeltsin's resistance gave the opposition a leader, a building and international support.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The crowd and the soldiers' refusal mattered as much as Yeltsin's leadership.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The coup revealed that the old structures had already unravelled.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The plotters held the key offices of state, so their failure was not inevitable.

howItGetsAsked: Evaluate the reasons for, and the consequences of, the failure of the August coup of 1991.

useItInAnEssay.claim: The August coup failed mainly because the forces the plotters commanded would not act for them.
useItInAnEssay.prove: Judt notes that a majority of senior KGB officers refused to back Kryuchkov, and the soldiers and elite KGB units sent into Moscow refused to fire on the demonstrators.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that the plotters held the offices of state but not the instruments of force, so Yeltsin's resistance at the White House could not be crushed.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, three demonstrators died on the night of 20–21 August, which shows that the outcome was not certain while the stand-off lasted.
useItInAnEssay.judge: The coup therefore failed because the state's own servants would not defend the state the plotters claimed to be saving.

chunks.title: From coup to dissolution, August–December 1991
chunks.body:
Gorbachev returned to a different country. Judt describes him speaking to the cameras about perestroika and the indispensable role the party would continue to play, while crowds at the Russian Parliament shouted that the party was "a criminal enterprise". He was humiliated by Yeltsin and the deputies. On 23 August Yeltsin suspended the Russian Communist Party, and within days Gorbachev resigned as General Secretary. Judt's verdict is that Gorbachev "had been overtaken by History and didn't know it".

The republics now left. Between 24 August and 21 September nine of them, including Ukraine and Belarus, declared independence; Ukraine's parliament voted on 24 August. Gorbachev replaced the Congress with a State Council of republic leaders, which approved Baltic independence and achieved little else. Yeltsin, meanwhile, took over the Union's institutions one by one: by November, Judt writes, he controlled virtually all financial and economic activity on Russian territory. On 24 October the KGB itself was abolished. The Soviet Union was becoming, in Judt's phrase, "a shell state".

**Ukraine** decided the outcome. On 1 December 1991 more than 92 per cent of Ukrainian voters approved independence, and Leonid Kravchuk, a former Communist boss turned nationalist, was elected president. Seventeen Moments calls the referendum "widely regarded as the decisive deathblow to the USSR": a Union without its second most populous republic made little sense to Russia either. A week later, on 8 December, Yeltsin, Kravchuk and the Belarusian leader Stanislav Shushkevich met at a hunting lodge in the Belovezha forest near Minsk, denounced the Union Treaty of 1922 and proposed a **Commonwealth of Independent States**. Gorbachev had not been consulted and called it "illegal and dangerous". On 21 December all the other republics except Georgia and the Baltic states declared their willingness to join. On 25 December Gorbachev resigned and the Russian flag replaced the Soviet one over the Kremlin. At midnight on 31 December 1991 the USSR ceased to exist.

Was this inevitable? Seventeen Moments argues that there was "no inevitability" about replacing the Union with the Commonwealth, a decision made "hastily if not whimsically". Archie Brown sees the disintegration as the ultimate unintended consequence of perestroika, but stresses what it left: fifteen independent states, and a Russia freer than at any point in its previous history. This mattered because the Union ended by agreement among its republics rather than by war, which meant that the collapse of a nuclear superpower was, for most of its territory, peaceful.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The coup's failure destroyed the party and handed the Union's power to Yeltsin's Russia.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Gorbachev remained President of the USSR until December, so the Union still had a legal centre.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Ukraine's referendum of 1 December was the decisive blow.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Russia's leaders had already taken over the Union's institutions, so Ukraine confirmed rather than caused the end.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The end of the Union was contingent, decided quickly by three leaders.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Judt's account of the shell state suggests that by December little was left to save.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: To what extent was the August coup responsible for the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991?

decodeKey.verb: To what extent: judge how far
decodeKey.scope: The dissolution of the Soviet Union
decodeKey.judgement: How far the coup, compared with Russian sovereignty, the republics and Gorbachev's concessions, caused the dissolution

modelPlan.thesis: The coup was largely responsible, because its failure destroyed the party and handed the Union's institutions to Yeltsin's Russia; but the republics' drive for sovereignty, sealed by Ukraine's vote, made the end final.

arguments.claim: The coup's failure discredited the party and the centre (named factor first).
Yeltsin used the aftermath to take over the Union's institutions.
The republics had been claiming sovereignty since 1990.
Ukraine's vote and Belovezha ended the Union.

modelPlan.counter: The Union Treaty would itself have reduced the centre to a shell, so the Union was ending by agreement before the coup.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Without the coup, would the Union have dissolved in 1991? Probably not: nine republics were about to sign a treaty, so the coup was the decisive cause of dissolution in 1991.

segments.text: The August coup was largely responsible for the dissolution of the Soviet Union, because its failure destroyed the authority of the centre it had tried to save.
After the coup collapsed on 21 August, Yeltsin suspended the Russian Communist Party, nine republics declared independence by 21 September, and the KGB was abolished on 24 October.
This meant that the party and the security services, the institutions that held the Union together, were discredited or dismantled, so Yeltsin's Russia could take over what remained.
However, Russia had claimed sovereignty in June 1990 and the Union Treaty would already have made republic laws supreme, so the centre was weakening before the coup.
The coup was therefore the decisive cause of dissolution in 1991, even though it accelerated a process already under way.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: “Yeltsin, not the coup plotters, destroyed the Soviet Union.” Discuss with reference to the period 1990 to 1991.
essayQuestions.scope: Soviet Union; responsibility for its end

decodeKey.verb: Discuss: test the claim for and against, then judge
decodeKey.scope: The destruction of the Soviet Union
decodeKey.judgement: How far Yeltsin, rather than the plotters, ended the Union

modelPlan.thesis: The claim is largely right: Yeltsin built Russia into a rival centre and dismantled the Union after August; but the plotters gave him the opportunity, and Ukraine's choice decided the end.

arguments.claim: Yeltsin made Russia a rival centre of power (named factor first).
After the coup Yeltsin took over the Union's institutions and co-founded the CIS.
The plotters' coup discredited the centre and the party.
Ukraine's referendum, not Yeltsin, was the decisive blow.

modelPlan.counter: Yeltsin joined the Novo-Ogarevo talks and planned to sign the Union Treaty, so before August he was willing to keep a looser Union.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Who removed the last chance of a Union? Yeltsin at Belovezha, but only after the plotters had destroyed the treaty and Ukraine had voted to leave.

segments.text: Yeltsin did more than the plotters to destroy the Soviet Union, because he turned the coup's failure into the dismantling of the centre.
By November 1991 he controlled virtually all financial and economic activity on Russian territory, and on 8 December he joined Kravchuk and Shushkevich in denouncing the Union Treaty of 1922.
This meant that the Union lost its largest republic's institutions and then its legal basis, so nothing remained for Gorbachev to govern.
However, Yeltsin had planned to sign the Union Treaty on 20 August; it was the plotters who destroyed it and discredited the centre.
The claim is therefore largely valid: the plotters created the opportunity, but Yeltsin used it to end the Union.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Evaluate the reasons for, and the consequences of, the failure of the August coup of 1991.

decodeKey.verb: Evaluate: weigh strengths and limits, then judge
decodeKey.scope: The failure of the August coup
decodeKey.judgement: Which reason mattered most, and which consequence was decisive

modelPlan.thesis: The coup failed mainly because the armed forces and KGB would not obey it; its most important consequence was the transfer of the Union's authority to Yeltsin's Russia, which made dissolution almost certain.

arguments.claim: Reason: the plotters lacked the support of the KGB and the army.
Reason: Yeltsin's resistance and the plotters' lack of a programme.
Consequence: the party discredited and suspended; Gorbachev overtaken.
Consequence: the republics declared independence and the Union became a shell.

modelPlan.counter: Yeltsin's leadership might be seen as the main reason, but without the soldiers' refusal his resistance would have been crushed.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which reason, if removed, would have let the coup succeed? The refusal of force: so it ranks first.

segments.text: The August coup failed mainly because the forces the plotters commanded would not act for them.
Judt notes that a majority of senior KGB officers refused to back Kryuchkov, and the soldiers sent into Moscow refused to fire on the demonstrators.
This meant that Yeltsin's stand at the White House could not be crushed, so the plotters lost their crucial asset, fear.
However, Yeltsin's leadership gave the resistance its focus and its international support, without which the refusal of force might not have been tested.
The refusal of force was therefore the decisive reason, and Yeltsin's resistance the decisive occasion.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Compare and contrast the roles of Gorbachev and Yeltsin in the collapse of the Soviet Union between 1990 and 1991.

decodeKey.verb: Compare and contrast: similarities and differences, explicitly linked
decodeKey.factorOrTask: The roles of Gorbachev and Yeltsin
decodeKey.scope: The collapse of the Soviet Union
decodeKey.judgement: Whose role was decisive, and why

modelPlan.thesis: Both weakened the centre, but in opposite ways: Gorbachev by conceding power to save the Union, Yeltsin by building Russia into a rival centre; Yeltsin's role became decisive after the coup.

arguments.claim: Similarity: both moved power from the centre to the republics.
Similarity: both negotiated the Union Treaty of 1991.
Difference: Yeltsin had a popular mandate and led the resistance; Gorbachev was elected by the Congress and held in the Crimea.
Difference: after the coup Gorbachev defended the party; Yeltsin suspended it and ended the Union.

modelPlan.counter: Gorbachev's earlier reforms made Yeltsin's rise possible, so the deepest role was Gorbachev's.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Whose actions ended the Union in 1991? Yeltsin's, at Belovezha, though Gorbachev's concessions had prepared the way.

segments.text: Gorbachev and Yeltsin both weakened the Soviet centre, but Gorbachev did so to save the Union and Yeltsin to replace it.

Gorbachev conceded the right of secession in April 1991 and negotiated a treaty giving the republics their resources, whereas Yeltsin declared Russian sovereignty in June 1990 and was elected President of Russia in June 1991.
This meant that Gorbachev gave away power to keep a Union, while Yeltsin gathered power for Russia, so the same process strengthened one and weakened the other.
However, both men took part in the Novo-Ogarevo talks, so until August their roles were more similar than their rivalry suggests.
The decisive difference came after the coup, when Yeltsin used his mandate to end the Union and Gorbachev could not stop him.

decodeKey.judgement: How far Ukraine's choice, compared with the coup and Russia, ended the Union

Belovezha followed one week later, with Kravchuk a co-founder of the CIS.
The coup had already discredited the centre.

modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Could a Union have survived without Ukraine? Not one Russia wanted, so Ukraine's vote was decisive for the form and timing of the end.

segments.text: Ukrainian independence was the decisive blow to the Soviet Union because it removed any basis for a renewed Union.
On 1 December 1991 more than 92 per cent of Ukrainian voters approved independence, and a week later Kravchuk joined Yeltsin at Belovezha to denounce the Union Treaty of 1922.
This meant that Russia's leaders faced a Union without its second most populous republic, so they chose a Commonwealth instead.
However, the Union was already a shell by November, with the KGB abolished and Yeltsin controlling economic activity in Russia.
Ukraine's independence was therefore decisive for the end of the Union in December 1991, though not its first cause.

segments.text: Gorbachev's Union Treaty failed mainly because the coup, launched to stop it, destroyed the centre that was to sign it.
The treaty was due to be signed on 20 August 1991, and the Emergency Committee seized power on 19 August.
This meant that the treaty's main supporter, Gorbachev, returned without authority, while the republics used the chaos to declare independence.
However, six republics had boycotted the March referendum, so even a signed treaty would not have kept the whole Union.
The coup was therefore the decisive reason the treaty failed, though the treaty could only ever have saved part of the Union.
